newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - HK firms borrow cheaply as handover nears.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK firms borrow cheaply as handover nears.

text.p: Hong Kong's blue chip borrowers are seeing funding costs fall as worries over the territory's return to China wane in the final months of British rule, bankers say.

"If you compare Hong Kong issuers with other issuers with the same credit rating, Hong Kong borrowers are still paying a premium and pricing still has some room to fall," said Peter Chan, senior vice president, syndications, at BA Asia.
"But now pricing is starting to come more in line because the so-called 1997 premium is declining," he said.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China on July 1, 1997.
Bankers said a healthy economy and buoyant real estate sector are contributing to a better market for the territory's borrowers, most of whom are property developers.
A fall-off in supply of new loans in second-half 1996 has created pent-up demand among lending banks, sources said.
But the major motivator behind narrower spreads is growing financial market optimism as the handover approaches, they added.
THE 1997 PREMIUM WANES

Local protesters and foreign leaders may decry Beijing's plans to dilute civil rights laws and scrap Hong Kong's elected legislature, but the mood in the financial markets has become increasingly bullish.

"The markets are a bit more sanguine about the handover than the politicians, perhaps because the markets don't have to concern themselves with the immediate fallout of human rights," said an analyst at a local bank.
"If there were a huge degree of political risk the markets would be worried. But so much of that has been discounted that there remains only the upside for the markets," he added.
Most pundits predict that China will allow Hong Kong to continue its laissez-faire way in financial matters because its wealth helps pave the way for a prosperous China.
"What's seen as favourable for one is increasingly being seen as favorable for the other," said the analyst.

Investors have also accepted that the Hong Kong dollar will remain pegged to the U.S. unit for the foreseeable future and that attempts to speculate against the local currency will not be tolerated by China or Hong Kong.

"The gap is closing because people had been worried about the availability of Hong Kong dollars, but this concern is dissipating now that we are in 1997," said the director of syndications at a European bank in Hong Kong.
SPREADS COMIMG IN
Property developer Cheung Kong Holdings has a HK$3.6 billion five-year amortising loan in the works that is widely expected to become a benchmark for this year's loan market.
The loan, which has an average life of four years, pays a return of 0.55 percent per annum to banks participating at the highest level, 20 basis points less than a similar deal in 1996.
Among other transactions that will be generally syndicated, Hysan Development is offering 0.64 percent per annum for its debut floating rate note, a HK$2.0 billion five-year issue.
That compares with the 0.75 percent spread paid by top borrower Sung Hung Kai last year for five-year financing.
Kerry Holdings also is in the market with a US$500 million loan that pays a leaner spread compared with its prior deals.
The story is the same in the international markets, where Hong Kong bond issues have performed well.

For example, the Mass Transit Railway Corp's (MTRC) Yankee bond due in October 2005 has been trading at 70-80 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries, in sharply from its 113 basis point spread at launch in 1995.
The MTRC is considered quasi-sovereign and has the same credit rating as Hong Kong with an A3 from Moody's Investors Service and Single-A from Standard and Poor's Corp.
"I think that investors see the quality of the Hong Kong names because the secondary trading prices have tightened a lot," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank.
In January, Dao Heng Bank placed 10-year subordinated bonds into the United States at 123 basis points over Treasuries, a far tighter spread than the 130-135 basis point gap expected.
China's bond issues also have done well. For example, China's global bond due in July 2006 is trading in the mid-70s over the benchmark versus 110 basis points at its launch last July.
Bankers said declining spreads in international markets offer Hong Kong corporates that traditionally have raised funds through syndicated loans a borrowing alternative.

"You are talking about some of the major corporates, especially the rated names, going to the Yankee market. That leads to competition in the loan market, which is another reason why spreads can't widen," said BA Asia's Chan.
Hutchison Whampoa and New World Infrastructure are widely rumoured to be eyeing the U.S. Yankee market.
BANKS TAKING A BEATING?
With spreads contracting, many bankers complain that it is becoming harder to take exposure to Hong Kong corporates.
Demand is strong now, but "it's just a matter of time before it hits the point where banks say no," to new loans, said a syndicate manager at a German bank.
It may be some time before the banks say no, however, because the same banks that are assuming the loans are arranging them from a different department.

"As a syndicate manager, I don't mind if the pricing gets lower and lower as long as I'm confident that the deal will get done. Of course, this view is not very popular with our portfolio managers that take the assets," said one banker.

While banks' corporate finance departments may feel a pinch, for the banking sector as a whole the narrowing spreads on corporate loans should have a modest effect on balance sheets because loans to firms make up a small share of loan portfolios.
"Loans to large corporates as a percentage of the total loan book has been steadily declining and will continue to do so," said Andrew Brown, a director at Salomon Brothers.

For one thing, Hong Kong borrowers are increasingly tapping different lenders through the capital markets. The lending banks, meanwhile, are turning to higher margin retail business, such as mortgage loans, insurance and credit cards, Brown said.

Lending banks may get a break later this year if, as expected, tighter spreads entice companies to borrow new money as well as re-finance. That would increase the supply of loans in the market and possibly curtail spread contraction.
